title: Investigators Linked Bank of New York Accounts to Semion Mogilevich in 1999
description_short: A 1999 investigation examined Russian funds moving through Bank of New York accounts linked to Semion Mogilevich.
description_medium: In August 1999, investigators examined billions of dollars moving through Bank of New York accounts amid suspicions of a Russian money-laundering operation. A New York Times report linked some accounts to businessman Semion Mogilevich. The supplied record establishes no connection between that investigation and Donald Trump.
description_long: In August 1999, investigators examined large transfers from Russia that had moved through accounts at the Bank of New York. A contemporaneous New York Times report described suspicious activity at the bank and linked certain accounts to businessman Semion Mogilevich. The linked timeline summarizes the story as a major money-laundering investigation, but the record does not provide a court finding that every transfer was criminal or that Mogilevich personally controlled each account. It also supplies no evidence connecting Donald Trump to the investigation. The event is therefore the scrutiny of Russian money flows through a major U.S. bank and the questions raised about who owned or controlled accounts, not a Trump business or campaign action. The distinction matters because the original title placed “Trump” before a banking story without documenting his involvement. This account keeps the focus on the reported investigation, identifies Mogilevich only as a person connected to some accounts in the reporting, and avoids turning suspicion into a finding of guilt. The source set does not establish the investigation’s final outcome.

title: Carter Page’s Moscow Meetings and Changing Accounts of Campaign Awareness
description_short: Trump adviser Carter Page met Russian officials in Moscow and later gave differing accounts of campaign awareness.
description_medium: Carter Page met Russian officials during a 2016 Moscow trip, including Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich and Rosneft figures, according to the linked timeline. Page later gave differing accounts of what meetings took place and who in the campaign knew about the trip. The record does not establish that those discrepancies amounted to a cover-up.
description_long: The linked Trumpfile timeline says Carter Page, then a Trump campaign foreign-policy adviser, traveled to Moscow in 2016 and met Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich, Rosneft investor-relations head Andrey Baranov and Rosneft chief Igor Sechin. It also says Page met Igor Diveykin, though Page denied meeting Sechin or Diveykin. The timeline describes changes in Page’s account of who knew about the trip: initially he said no one in the campaign knew, then that staff learned after he returned, and later he told the House Intelligence Committee that J.D. Gordon, Corey Lewandowski, Hope Hicks and Jeff Sessions knew beforehand. Page reportedly emailed Trump officials afterward with a “readout” of insights from Russian officials. These are the timeline’s account of the meetings and later disclosures, with some claims attributed to Christopher Steele or Page himself. They show why the trip drew scrutiny, but the page alone does not establish that Page concealed the meetings or prove campaign coordination with Russia.

title: U.S. Transferred Venezuelan Migrants to El Salvador Under the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025
description_short: In March 2025, the U.S. sent nearly 300 people to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act, including 238 Venezuelans.
description_medium: On March 15, 2025, DHS sent nearly 300 people to El Salvador under Trump’s invocation of the Alien Enemies Act. The American Immigration Council reported that 238 Venezuelans were accused largely on the basis of tattoos and 23 Salvadorans were accused of MS-13 ties; more than 130 Venezuelans had pending hearings and no removal orders.
description_long: The Trump administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025 to remove Venezuelan men it alleged were members of the Tren de Aragua gang. The American Immigration Council reported that on March 15, officials sent nearly 300 people on three planes to El Salvador, including 238 Venezuelans accused largely on the basis of tattoos and 23 Salvadorans accused of belonging to MS-13. More than 130 of the Venezuelans had pending immigration hearings and had not received removal orders under the usual immigration process, according to the report. The transfers were made under the 1798 wartime statute and an agreement with El Salvador. The report said people on the planes were not told what was happening or given an opportunity to challenge the allegations before transfer. It raises due-process concerns about the use of secret gang accusations. The documented event is the March transfer; these sources do not establish indefinite detention or family camps.
subcategory: Indefinite Detention and Due Process Suspension

title: Trump Order Directs Smithsonian Exhibit Review and Changes to Historical Presentation
description_short: Trump’s March 2025 order directed review of Smithsonian exhibits and historical presentation; removal is not documented.
description_medium: Trump’s March 27, 2025 executive order, “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” criticized Smithsonian presentations about race and named “The Shape of Power.” It assigned the vice president a role in reviewing exhibitions and allowed potential changes, but the linked page does not document that the exhibit or Black-history materials were removed.
description_long: On March 27, 2025, Trump signed the executive order “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” The order criticized the Smithsonian Institution for what it called divisive, race-centered ideology and cited “The Shape of Power: Stories of Race and American Sculpture,” an exhibition examining race in the United States. According to the linked account, the order gave the vice president a role in reviewing exhibitions and potentially eliminating those the administration considered inconsistent with its view of American history. It also directed the vice president to work with Congress on Smithsonian appropriations, called for reinstating monuments removed since 2020, and restricted descriptions of historical figures that condemn them. These directives place pressure on how the Smithsonian and federal monuments present race and national history. The source does not show that the named exhibition was taken down or that Black-history displays were removed. The title is limited to the review and presentation requirements in the order, not a claim that removals had already occurred.

description_short: Trump Approval Craters to 36-38% — 74% of Americans Say Iran War Not Worth the Cost

It reports 36% approval and 59% disapproval in an Economist/YouGov tracker, a 38% approval average in the New York Times polling compilation, and a CNN/SSRS finding that 74% of respondents considered the Iran war not worth its cost. Poll results can indicate public sentiment at a point in time, but comparisons depend on field dates, samples, and question wording. Those methodological details are not supplied for the reported figures, and the packet does not establish that the cited survey results caused any policy change.

title: SSA Inspector General Reviews Whistleblower Allegations About DOGE Data
description_short: NPR reported separate watchdog and congressional inquiries into allegations that a former DOGE worker retained Social Security data.
description_medium: NPR reported on March 11, 2026, that the Social Security Administration’s inspector general was reviewing an anonymous complaint about possible data misuse by a former DOGE employee. Separately, congressional Democrats expanded an inquiry after a whistleblower alleged that a former SSA software engineer retained sensitive databases and planned to share them with a private employer. NPR had not reviewed the complaint.
description_long: NPR reported on March 11, 2026, that the Social Security Administration’s inspector general was reviewing an anonymous complaint about potential misuse of agency data by a former Department of Government Efficiency employee. Congressional Democrats separately expanded their inquiry after receiving whistleblower information about a former DOGE software engineer who allegedly retained copies of the NUMIDENT and Death Master File. The NUMIDENT contains Social Security numbers, birth information, and parents’ names for nearly every living American; the Death Master File contains records of people reported deceased. The whistleblower alleged that one database was kept on a personal thumb drive, that the former staffer claimed “God-level” system access, and that the employee planned to share data with a new private-sector employer. NPR said it had not reviewed the complaint, and the story reports investigations into allegations rather than official findings that data was retained or transferred. The scope of any retained records and any planned disclosure remained unverified in the report.
subcategory: Social Security Data Access and Oversight
notes: NPR confirms a review of an anonymous complaint and a separate congressional inquiry based on whistleblower claims. The revised title and descriptions explicitly attribute data retention and planned disclosure to allegations; the story reports no finding that the data was retained or transferred.
